title: Flexora: should the price go up to $75?
prompt: Flexora sells scheduling and billing software to independent gyms across the US. It charges $60 per gym per month and has 5,000 customers. The CEO wants to raise the price to $75 for everyone. Should the company do it? How would you approach this?

facts.answer: 5,000 gyms each pay $60 a month. Everyone pays the same price, on month-to-month contracts that can be cancelled at any time.
Customers range from small studios with under 200 members to clubs with more than 1,000. All of them pay the same $60 today. There is no data on how willingness to pay differs by gym size.

Each gym costs Flexora about $15 a month to serve (support, hosting and reminder messages to members), whatever the price. Fixed costs, such as the product team and offices, do not change with the price either. A breakdown is available.

The CEO wants to maximise monthly contribution (revenue minus variable costs). There is no hard limit on customer losses, but the CEO worries that losing many gyms at once would hurt referrals, which bring in most new customers.
Two competitors sell similar products to US gyms, at $55 and $80 a month. The $80 product has more features; the $55 product is simpler.

Last month Flexora surveyed 600 of its customers, a mix of small and large gyms. It asked whether they would stay or cancel within three months if the price rose to each of four higher prices. The results are available.
Customers can cancel any month, but moving to another system takes a gym a few weeks of effort.
About 1.5% of customers cancel in a typical month at today's price. Assume that rate stays the same at any of the tested prices, on top of the one-off loss the survey shows.
New customers come mainly from referrals and search. Assume a price change does not change how many new customers join in the next six months.
No new features are planned in the next six months.
Flexora's contracts give existing customers 30 days' notice of a price change. Flexora can change the price for everyone at once or for a chosen group of customers, for example to test it.

key_buckets: Customers: willingness to pay and likely cancellations at each price
Company economics: contribution per customer and the break-even customer loss
Implementation options: one price, tiers or staged rises
good_signs: Works with contribution (price minus variable cost), not just revenue
Calculates the break-even customer loss before looking at the survey
Compares more than one price point instead of only $60 versus $75
Asks what the survey measured (who answered, over what period) and questions how reliable stated intentions are
red_flags: Looks only at revenue and ignores the $15 variable cost
Accepts the survey at face value
Backs $75 because contribution rises, without noticing that the expected 22% loss is close to the 25% break-even

exhibits.title: Variable cost to serve one gym ($ per month)

rows: Text and email reminders to members

exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask what it costs Flexora to serve each gym, or for the variable cost per customer.
exhibits.insight: Variable cost per gym is $15 a month, so each gym contributes $45 today ($60 minus $15). None of it changes with the price, so every extra dollar of price is extra contribution.

exhibits.title: Survey of 600 customers: share who would stay at each price
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask what the customer research says about how many customers would stay at higher prices.
exhibits.insight: Retention falls slowly up to $70 and then faster. At $75, 22% say they would leave, close to the 25% break-even; at $70, 12% would leave against an 18% break-even; at $80, 38% would leave.

math.question: If the price rises from $60 to $75, what is the largest percentage of customers Flexora could lose and still make at least today's monthly contribution?
math.working: Contribution per gym rises from $45 to $60. Keeping total contribution equal needs 45 / 60 = 75% of customers, so up to 25% could leave. Shortcut: the $15 price rise divided by the new contribution of $60 is 25%.

math.question: What is Flexora's monthly contribution today, in dollars?
Using the survey, what would monthly contribution be at $75, in dollars?
math.working: 78% of 5,000 is 3,900 gyms. Each contributes $75 - $15 = $60. 3,900 x $60 = $234,000, which is 4% above today. Revenue falls, though, from $300,000 to $292,500.

math.question: Using the survey, what would monthly contribution be at $70, in dollars?
math.working: 88% of 5,000 is 4,400 gyms. Each contributes $70 - $15 = $55. 4,400 x $55 = $242,000, which is 7.6% above today and $8,000 above the $75 option.

math.question: At $70 instead, what is the largest percentage of customers Flexora could lose and still make at least today's monthly contribution?
math.working: Contribution per gym rises from $45 to $55, so Flexora needs 45 / 55 = about 82% of customers to stay: it could lose up to about 18%. The survey expects 12% to leave at $70, a margin of about 6 points, against only 3 points at $75 (22% expected versus 25% break-even).

brainstorm.question: Besides one price change for everyone, what else could Flexora do to earn more from its customers?
idea_bank: Create tiers such as Basic and Pro, so larger or more demanding gyms pay more
Charge by gym size or number of members
Offer a discount for paying a year in advance, which also reduces cancellations
Raise prices in two steps (for example $65, then $70) and watch cancellations
Protect long-standing customers with a smaller rise
Add paid extras such as marketing tools or a member app
Take a small share of the member payments processed through the platform
Test a new price on new customers or a sample of existing ones first
Improve onboarding and support to reduce cancellations at any price

must_mention: Not $75: the break-even loss is 25% and the survey suggests 22% would leave, so contribution rises only slightly ($234k versus $225k) with little room for error
$70 is the best of the tested prices: about $242k a month versus $225k today, with more room for error (break-even at an 18% loss against 12% expected)
Survey answers are not the same as real behaviour, so test before rolling out to everyone
good_signs: Recommends about $70, or a staged increase with monitoring
Puts the gain in yearly terms: about $17k a month, or roughly $200k a year
Considers the effect on referrals and new customers, not only this month's contribution
Notes that $75 would sit close to the $80 competitor, which has more features
Proposes a test on a group of customers and the measures to track

model_answer_outline: Clarify the objective: maximise monthly contribution without losing so many gyms that referrals suffer. Confirm the $15 variable cost, that normal cancellations stay at 1.5% a month, and that new-customer numbers are unaffected.
Structure: customers' willingness to pay, Flexora's economics, competitors and alternatives, how to implement, risks.
Break-even first: at $75, contribution per gym rises from $45 to $60, so Flexora can lose up to 25% of customers before it is worse off.

Survey: at $75, 78% stay, so contribution is $234k versus $225k today (+4%), but the expected 22% loss is only 3 points short of break-even. At $70, 88% stay and contribution is $242k (+7.6%), with a break-even loss of 18% against 12% expected. At $65 it is $237.5k; at $80 it falls to $201.5k.
Insight: the biggest and safest gain comes from a smaller rise than the CEO proposed. Revenue alone would mislead: at $75 revenue falls ($292.5k versus $300k) even though contribution rises.

Recommendation: do not go to $75. Move to about $70 (worth about $17k a month, roughly $200k a year), testing it on a group of customers first and giving 30 days' notice; consider a smaller step for the longest-standing gyms. Track cancellations weekly against the 12% the survey implies, and referrals and new sign-ups monthly.
